messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Vignette:
Asha was 44, married, and had spent most of her adult life working in retail in a busy store where she was expected to stay on her feet, keep track of customers, and respond quickly when problems came up. Before the event that brought her to treatment, she had been known at work as calm, obliging, and hard to rattle. That changed after she witnessed a sudden, disturbing incident that she has struggled to put in order ever since. Even now, when she tries to tell it, the story comes out in fragments. She knows what happened was real, but the sequence slips away from her; she finds herself moving from one image to another without being able to line them up properly. What stays with her is the feeling of being overwhelmed at the time and the sense that everything happened too fast for her to make sense of it.

In the weeks after the event, Asha noticed that her attention began to go constantly outward, as though she needed to keep watch on every corner of whatever room she was in. In the store, she found herself scanning the aisles, the entrance, and the faces of customers for any sign that something was not right. She said she was “always looking,” even when nothing was happening, and that she could not relax unless she knew where people were and what they were doing. The habit followed her home as well. In public places she chose seats where she could see the door, and when she was with others she tended to agree quickly with what they wanted, because going along with them felt safer than expressing a preference. This people-pleasing was not how she had always been, but it became her default way of getting through the day, especially when she felt uncertain about who around her could be trusted.

Certain moments set off a sudden rush of distress. If someone in the store started crying, Asha would feel a sharp jolt and have to turn away. The sound and sight of tears seemed to pull her straight back toward the memory, not in a clear story but in a wave of feeling she could not control. She also became uneasy when she felt dizzy or lightheaded, because that bodily sensation reminded her of the physical helplessness she experienced during and after the trauma. Those moments could make her feel as if she needed to sit down immediately, and she described a brief panic that something terrible was about to happen again. Talking about the event was the hardest trigger of all. Even before she finished a sentence, she would feel the pressure building in her chest and throat, and there were times when she had to stop mid-sentence because the emotional force of the memory became too much.

As time went on, Asha lived with a nearly constant sense of being on guard. She described herself as superalert, watchful, and easily startled, as if her body had learned to stay braced for danger. In the store, a sudden movement at the edge of her vision or an unexpected voice behind her made her jump. She found herself turning quickly to check who was there, and she was embarrassed by how tense she had become in ordinary situations. At home too, she remained keyed up, continually checking her surroundings, as though missing a detail could put her or her family at risk. These habits became tiring, but she felt unable to let them go. She believed that if she stopped watching closely, she might be caught off guard in the same way she was before.

Asha also spent a great deal of time trying to understand why the event had happened to her. She kept returning to it in her mind, asking herself what it meant and why she had been there to witness it at all. She did not experience these thoughts as comforting; rather, they became another painful place she could not leave. When she remembered the event, what came most strongly was grief. She would be flooded with it so intensely that she had to stop what she was doing, sometimes putting down her work or leaving a conversation because the feeling became overwhelming. At those times, the memory itself felt disorganized and unbearable: the details would not settle into a clear order, but the sorrow attached to them was unmistakable.

By the time she sought help, Asha was still working, but she was exhausted by how much effort it took to keep herself composed at work and in public. Her marriage and daily routines had narrowed around avoiding anything that might set off the memories or expose her to situations where she felt unprepared. She came to treatment because the constant alertness, the startle, the dizzy spells, and the overwhelming grief were no longer things she could simply push through. What she most hoped for was some way to remember what happened without being overwhelmed by it, and what she most feared was that if she let down her guard, something frightening would happen again before she could react.
